title: An Accusation in a Hall and a Page of Errata
subtitle: The Seventh Night, the Eighth Day, and What the Fair Copy Says

setting.name: The Reckoning House, Days Seven and Eight
setting.description: The last two days. The House knows the couriers come up at thaw and that whatever is decided before then is what goes down the pass with them. Upstairs, the fair copy of the Almanac lies on the Master's desk in a sealed quire-case waiting for a seal that no longer has an owner. In the hall, the orrery stands with a weight on the wrong hook. In the drying loft, over the kitchen flue, a lamp gets knocked into a pile of dry linen on the seventh evening and the House has ninety seconds to decide whether it has a building. And on the seventh night, if nobody has said her name, Ilsabet Wray puts on her coat and goes out through the postern into a pass that has already very nearly killed a fitter person than her.
setting.atmosphere: The end of something. Wet wool, lamplight, and eleven people who have been awake too long and are about to find out whether they can go back to work in the spring. The fire in the loft is the campaign's last physical danger and it is over in four minutes. Everything after it is people in a room. The final scene is an accusation made out loud in a stone hall by lamplight in front of everybody who lives here, and a woman of fifty-four coming apart very quietly in a chair, and then a page of arithmetic being corrected — and the campaign should end on the arithmetic, not the collapse.

keyLocations.name: The Drying Loft
keyLocations.description: Under the roof, over the kitchen flue, with everything the House owns that has been washed this week hanging on lines. Warm, dry, full of linen, and lit by lamps because there are no windows. Set-piece three of three.
features: Lines of dry linen, House-coats and blankets, four feet from a flue that runs hot
One way down: a ladder stair through a hatch in the floor
The C4 coat, if the party did not take it, which burns
encounters: The fire itself, which starts by accident on the seventh evening and is not arson
Getting Nan Gaddy out, who is up there when it starts
Losing whatever evidence is still stored in the loft
secrets: It is genuinely an accident: a lamp on a beam, knocked by a hand reaching for a blanket, on a night when the whole House is exhausted. The DM must not turn it into arson under any circumstances
Ilsabet Wray goes up the ladder for Nan Gaddy without hesitating, which is the last thing the party learns about her before they name her

keyLocations.name: The Postern, on the Seventh Night
keyLocations.description: The door in the yard wall, and beyond it a pass that took a fit young courier and nearly kept him. If nobody has named her by the seventh night, Ilsabet Wray goes out through it.
features: A postern that is barred at night by a boy who now never forgets
Snow to the top of the wall on the outer side
One set of small bootprints, going out, and no set coming back
encounters: Finding her gone, which happens at about four in the morning
Going out after her, which is a genuine risk to the party
secrets: She is not running. There is nowhere to run to and she knows it better than anyone in the building
If she is brought back in she does not resist and does not explain, and she is markedly easier to speak to afterwards

keyLocations.name: The Hall, on the Eighth Evening
keyLocations.description: Where the accusation is made. Everybody present, because everybody is always present at the long table, and the orrery standing at the far end with its brass catching the fire.
features: Twelve residents, the party, one long table and four storeys of dark above it
The sun-weight, which can be taken off the wrong hook and put on the table
Sennet Vole in his chair, who can time the whole evening of the second night by the chimes if anyone asks him to
encounters: The accusation, and whom it is made against
Ilsabet Wray's collapse, if C3 and C8 are presented together
The wrong accusation, and what the House does with it
secrets: She confesses to C3 and C8 together and to nothing less: not to intimidation, not to a good Persuasion roll alone, not to being cornered
The confession is a collapse and not a speech, and she is to be played with pity

keyLocations.name: The Master's Desk and the Fair Copy
keyLocations.description: The last scene of the campaign. A sealed quire-case, a fair copy of the Almanac with three years of false frost dates behind it, and a decision about a page of errata that has to be made by the House rather than by the party.
features: The fair copy, complete, four hundred pages in a clerk's hand, ready for the courier
Ardwen's three errata drafts, naming the House and no individual
The Archivist's seal, which is the only seal left in the building
encounters: Persuading the House to bind an errata sheet into its own Almanac
Halva Onn, who has to decide whether her seal can stand in for the Master's
Writing the correction, which requires C5 and preferably C6
secrets: The harvest can be saved even if the murder is never solved, and the murder can be solved with the harvest lost. The DM must not let one resolve the other
If Ilsabet Wray is still in the building and still able to work, she is the best person in the province to compute the correction, and she will do it

synopsis: Two days left. On the seventh evening a lamp goes into the linen in the drying loft and the House has ninety seconds to decide whether it still has a building — an accident, not arson, and the last physical danger in the campaign. On the seventh night, if nobody has said her name, Ilsabet Wray puts on her coat and goes out through the postern into the pass. And on the eighth evening the party makes an accusation, out loud, in a stone hall, in front of everybody who lives here. Present C3 and C8 together and she confesses, and it is a collapse rather than a speech, and it is hard to watch. Present anything less and she does not, whatever the roll. Accuse the wrong person and the riders take them at thaw and the story continues, because it does not reset. Then, whatever has happened, there is a fair copy on a desk with three years of false frost dates behind it and a printer eleven days past thaw, and somebody has to write a page of errata — and the campaign ends on the arithmetic, not on the confession.
hook: On the seventh morning somebody counts the days out loud at breakfast for the first time since this started — Halva Onn, flatly, into her tea, as if it were a tide table: 'Thaw is Tuesday. The riders will be up by Thursday. So we have two days to be a House that has decided something, and after that we are a House that had a thing decided about it.' Nobody answers her. Merrit Doane opens his mouth and, for the first time in six days, closes it again. And at the far end of the table, Ilsabet Wray finishes her tea, puts the cup down without a sound, and goes up to her desk to work, because the eastern hundreds' tide tables for the third quarter are not going to compute themselves and somebody in this building still has to do the arithmetic.

acts.title: Act 1: Fire in the Loft
acts.description: Set-piece three of three, and the last physical danger in the campaign. It starts by accident, it lasts four minutes, it may destroy evidence, and it shows the party one more thing about Ilsabet Wray immediately before they name her.
objectives: Get Nan Gaddy down the ladder
Stop the fire before it reaches the roof timbers
Save whatever evidence is stored in the loft, if any
Notice who went up the ladder first

scenes.name: Ninety Seconds
scenes.description: A lamp on a beam, a hand reaching for a blanket, and four minutes that decide whether this building exists in the spring.
scenes.readAloud: "It is about eight in the evening and everybody is exhausted in the particular way of people who have been being careful around each other for six days, and Nan Gaddy has gone up to the loft for blankets for the courier. Then there is a noise from the hatch that is not a word, and a light up there that is the wrong colour, and then the smell arrives in the hall all at once — not smoke, at first; hot linen, which is a smell everybody in this House knows and nobody has ever been frightened of before. Somebody is already at the ladder. Somebody else is shouting for the yard buckets. And Wat Ormery, who is the only person in the hall who has ever seen a building burn, says one thing in a voice that cuts through everything: 'Not water on the flue — get the LINEN DOWN!'"

skillChecks.success: You get up the ladder into the smoke and start hauling lines down bodily, which is the correct answer: the fire is in the hanging linen and not yet in the timbers, and stripping the lines starves it.
skillChecks.failure: You get up there and the smoke takes you: DC 12 Constitution save or 2d6 damage and you come down the ladder faster than you went up. The fire reaches the first roof timber.

skillChecks.success: Nan Gaddy is down at the far end behind the lines, on the floor, not moving much, and nobody else has seen her.
skillChecks.failure: Smoke, heat, and a great many people shouting at each other on a ladder.

skillChecks.success: You know how a roof fire runs and you cut the lines in the right order, working from the flue outward, and the whole thing is over in four minutes with a scorched loft and no structural damage.
skillChecks.failure: It takes eleven minutes and two roof timbers and the loft is gutted. Everything stored up there is gone.

skillChecks.success: Gaddy has taken a lungful and a burn to one arm and will be fine in a fortnight, and she should not be moved quickly, and you know it.
skillChecks.failure: She is breathing. That is as much as you can establish in a yard full of shouting people.

scenes.roleplayNotes: IT IS AN ACCIDENT AND THE DM MUST NOT MAKE IT ARSON. There is no attempt to destroy evidence here and no second crime in this campaign; a lamp was knocked off a beam by a tired woman reaching for a blanket. If the party investigates it — and they will — the honest answer is available on a DC 12 Investigation and it is 'a lamp, a beam, and a hand.' Say it plainly. IF THE C4 COAT IS STILL IN THE LOFT, IT BURNS, and the DM should let it burn and say so; the case does not depend on it.

scenes.name: Who Went Up First
scenes.description: A short scene afterwards, in the yard, in the cold, with everybody standing about coughing. The last thing the party learns about Ilsabet Wray before they name her.
scenes.readAloud: "Afterwards everybody stands about in the yard in the cold because nobody can face going back inside yet, and the counting-up happens the way it always does: who is hurt, what is lost, what it will cost. Nan Gaddy is sitting on an upturned tub with a blanket round her being told off by the cook. The loft is scorched and the roof held. And somebody says — Wat Ormery, to nobody in particular, in the tone of a man who noticed something at the time and has only now had a moment to think about it — 'Ilsabet went up first. Straight up, before any of us. Got her out from behind the lines.' And she is standing about eight feet away with soot on her face and she does not say anything at all, because there is nothing to say to that, and because she is fifty-four and tired and has been holding one thing in her head for six days."

skillChecks.success: She is not performing. She went up the ladder because somebody was up there, without a thought in her head about how it would look, and she is standing here now realising that people are going to say she is a good woman, and that is the worst thing that has happened to her this week.
skillChecks.failure: A woman with soot on her face who has just done something brave.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene exists so that the accusation costs something. She is not a monster: she is exhausted, frightened, and the first person up the ladder, and the players should have to carry both of those things into the hall tomorrow evening. Do not undercut it, do not have her behave suspiciously afterwards, and do not let anybody comment on the irony.

acts.title: Act 2: The Seventh Night
acts.description: If nobody has said her name by the seventh night, Ilsabet Wray goes out through the postern into the pass. This act is optional in the sense that a party who is already certain may skip it entirely — and it is the failure state beginning, and the DM should run it exactly as written.
objectives: Discover that she is gone, at about four in the morning
Decide whether to go out after her, in the dark, into a pass that nearly killed a courier
Bring her back, or do not

scenes.name: The Bar Off the Postern
scenes.description: Four in the morning, a postern standing open, and one set of small bootprints going out with nothing coming back.
scenes.readAloud: "It is Jory Pike who finds it, at about four in the morning, because Jory Pike has barred that postern every night of his life since somebody died and he does not sleep well any more and he came down to check it for the third time. The bar is off. The door is standing about a foot open with the snow blown in across the flags in a long white fan. And on the outer side, out into the dark, going away from the House, there is one set of small bootprints with a squared heel, and nothing at all coming back."

skillChecks.success: You can follow them, in the dark, if you go now and go roped. They are perhaps twenty minutes old. Beyond three hundred yards the wind has them and the drift starts, and after that it is guesswork and a lantern.
skillChecks.failure: They are gone within sixty yards. There is a wind and there is a great deal of country out there and you cannot track anything in this.

skillChecks.success: Same boot as the landing, if the party got C9 on the first day. Small, squared heel. It is the only physical thing in the entire campaign that connects that stair to a person, and it is standing in the snow of the yard being blown away as you look at it.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody's boots. Everybody in this House has boots.

scenes.roleplayNotes: SHE IS NOT ESCAPING. There is nowhere to go and she knows the pass better than anyone in the building. If the party goes after her within the hour they find her about four hundred yards out, sitting down, not moving, having stopped because stopping was always what this was. She comes back without resisting and without explaining. If they do not go, or do not find her, she is found at thaw and the failure state runs. Do not narrate her intent and do not let any NPC speculate about it.

scenes.name: Four Hundred Yards
scenes.description: Going out after her, at night, roped, into the first of the drift. A short, cold, entirely non-combat scene with real risk to the party.
scenes.readAloud: "Four hundred yards is nothing. Four hundred yards is the length of the village street at home. Four hundred yards out here at four in the morning with a lantern and a rope is forty minutes of putting one leg into snow up to the thigh and taking it out again, with the wind coming across the shoulder of the hill hard enough that the man behind you is a shape and not a person. And then the lantern finds her. She is sitting down in it, with her back against a rock, with her coat on and her hands in her lap and her eyes open, and she has been there long enough to be very cold and not long enough to be dying, and when the light comes onto her face she says — not startled, not frightened, in the voice of somebody continuing a conversation — 'I couldn't do it. I sat down instead. I've been sitting here trying to make myself get up and go on and I can't do that either.'"

skillChecks.success: You get her up and back, roped, without losing anybody. Forty minutes out and fifty-five back with a woman who cannot walk properly.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone who went out gains a level of exhaustion and one character makes a DC 13 Constitution save or takes 2d6 cold damage. You still get back.

skillChecks.success: She keeps her fingers. Warm slowly, out of the wind, no fire and no spirits, exactly as with the courier.
skillChecks.failure: She keeps her hands and loses the ends of two toes, which she does not mention to anybody for a fortnight.

scenes.roleplayNotes: SHE DOES NOT CONFESS HERE. Whatever she says in the snow, and whatever she says in the room they put her in afterwards, she does not confess to a party who has not put C3 and C8 in front of her. She is much easier to talk to after this — she answers questions she previously deflected, and she will place herself in the study at a quarter past eight without being pushed — but the confession still requires the two clues together. Hold that line even when the scene makes it tempting not to.

acts.title: Act 3: The Eighth Evening
acts.description: The accusation, in the hall, in front of everybody. The confession, if it is earned. The failure state, if it is not. And then the arithmetic, which is where the campaign ends.
objectives: Make an accusation, out loud, in front of the House
Present C3 and C8 together, or do not
Deal with what happens either way
Get a page of errata into the fair copy before the couriers come up

scenes.name: The Accusation
scenes.description: The whole House at the long table on the eighth evening, and the party standing up. This scene is the campaign and it should be given as much table time as it wants.
scenes.readAloud: "They are all there because they are always all there; that is what the long table is. Twelve of them, and the lamps, and four storeys of dark going up above the beams, and the orrery down at the end with its brass catching the fire. Nobody has to be assembled. Nobody has to be told what this is. Halva Onn puts her cup down. Merrit Doane, for once in his life, is entirely silent. Sennet Vole opens his eyes, which he has not done in front of anybody in four days. And Oriel Fenn, who has fed every person in this room three times a day for six days while they suspected each other, stops in the doorway with a dish in her hands and does not put it down."

skillChecks.success: The House hears you out properly instead of arguing over you, which is worth a great deal: you get to lay the whole case out in order, and by the end of it eleven people have followed it and know where it is going before you get there.
skillChecks.failure: You are interrupted four times and the room fractures and you have to make the accusation into a shouting match, which does not change the outcome but makes it uglier for everybody, including the accused.

skillChecks.success: You lay out the chain in the right order — the lamp, the weight, the coat, the body, the page — and it holds together in front of an audience of people who compute for a living and will spot a gap instantly.
skillChecks.failure: You have the pieces and you present them badly, and Halva Onn finds two holes in your ordering that are not holes in your case, and you have to go round again.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THE CONFESSION REQUIRES C3 AND C8 PRESENTED TOGETHER AND NOTHING LESS. Not a natural 20 on Persuasion. Not intimidation. Not being cornered. Not a player simply naming her correctly. If the party has C3 (struck, then moved) and C8 (his own account of what he told her and what it would cost her) and puts both in front of her in that room, she confesses. If they have only one, she does not — she says 'no' quietly and sits with her hands in her lap and nothing in the world moves her, and the party has one more night and then the riders come. If C8 was lost in the ash-pan, the substitute is C3 plus Sennet Vole placing the study argument by the chimes plus the timeline reconstructed — the DM should accept that combination, because it is the same weight of evidence assembled a harder way, and refusing it would punish the party for a clock that was always going to expire on somebody.

scenes.name: A Collapse, Not a Speech
scenes.description: Ilsabet Wray confesses. Play it with pity, keep it short, and do not let her explain herself well.
scenes.readAloud: "She does not stand up. That is the first thing, and it is somehow the worst: she stays sitting with her hands flat on the table on either side of her cup, and she looks at the page — the burned page, the brown lace of it, his handwriting — for a long time, longer than anybody in the room can stand. And then she says, 'I asked him for a season. One season, to correct it quietly, and no one would ever have known and the tables would have been right.' She is not looking at anybody. 'And he said there was no time and he was going to bind it in and put his own name to it, and I thought — ' and she stops, and her hands are not steady, and she puts them in her lap. 'I went up to ask him again. That was all it was. I went up the servants' stair to ask him again, and he did not turn round.' And that is the whole of it. She does not say the rest, and nobody in that hall makes her."
scenes.roleplayNotes: SHORT. She does not have a monologue, she does not justify herself well, and she does not name the reason as pride even though it was. The room does not react loudly: this is a House of people who have known each other twenty years and the sound they make is not a gasp. Oriel Fenn puts the dish down. Sennet Vole closes his eyes again. Merrit Doane, who has been wrong at the top of his voice for six days, starts to cry, which nobody expected including him. There is no trial, no execution scene, no arrest, and no restraint — she goes to her room and Wat Ormery sits outside it, and she does not try the door.

scenes.name: The Wrong Name
scenes.description: The failure branch. If the party accuses someone else and it sticks, run this, and do not reset anything.
scenes.readAloud: "They accept it. That is the thing you are least prepared for. You lay it out and it is coherent and it is wrong, and eleven exhausted people who want an answer more than they want the right one look at each other and take it, because the alternative is going down that pass in two days without one. The accused says whatever they say — protests, or does not, or says something quiet and dignified that you will think about for years — and it does not matter, because the room has decided, and the room is the only court there is up here. Wat Ormery sits outside their door. Oriel Fenn cooks. And on the seventh night, or the eighth, or at thaw, Ilsabet Wray goes out through the postern."
scenes.roleplayNotes: THE STORY CONTINUES; IT DOES NOT RESET. Run the caseFile's failureState as written. The riders take the accused at thaw. Wray attempts the postern and either dies in the pass or is found and lives with her health broken. If she lives, a letter reaches the party about two years later from Halva Onn, enclosing a page in Wray's hand. Do not give the party a second chance at the accusation, do not have an NPC intervene with the truth, and do not soften it at the last moment. A fair-play mystery that cannot be lost was never fair.

scenes.name: The Fair Copy
scenes.description: The last scene of the campaign, and it is about arithmetic. A sealed quire-case, three years of false frost dates, a printer eleven days past thaw, and a page of errata that the House has to agree to bind into its own Almanac.
scenes.readAloud: "The fair copy is four hundred pages in a clerk's hand in a quire-case on the Master's desk, and it has been ready since the first frost. Behind it, in three of its columns, are the eastern hundreds' frost dates, nine days late, three years running. And the argument that happens in the hall on the last night is not about a murder at all: it is about whether this House will bind a page into its own Almanac saying that it was wrong. Halva Onn holds the only seal left in the building and will not use it lightly. Corwin Tace, who is ruined and knows it, says — because he is the only person here who has already lost everything and therefore the only one with nothing to weigh — 'Bind it in. What have we got to protect? Him? He wrote it himself.'"

skillChecks.success: The House votes to bind the errata in. Halva Onn's seal goes on it in place of the Master's, which is not strictly permitted and which she does anyway, and she writes a line under it saying exactly what she has done and why so that whoever comes after her knows.
skillChecks.failure: The House cannot agree in one evening and the fair copy goes down as it stands. The eastern hundreds plant nine days early on a printed frost date and lose the crop, and the campaign closes on that, narrated as a consequence and not as a punishment.

skillChecks.success: With C5 and C6 you can write the correction itself, correctly, and it will hold up in front of a printer who has been doing this for thirty years.
skillChecks.failure: You can prove the dates are wrong and you cannot supply the right ones, which means the errata says 'do not trust these tables' rather than 'the date is the ninth', which saves about half the crop.

skillChecks.success: If Ilsabet Wray is still in the building and still able to work, she is the best computer in the province and she will do the correction if asked, and asking her is a decision the party has to make with everybody watching.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody in this House can do the arithmetic and you cannot think who.

scenes.roleplayNotes: END THE CAMPAIGN HERE, ON THE ARITHMETIC. Not on the confession, not on the riders, not on a summary of who was right. If the party asks Ilsabet Wray to compute the correction — and it is the single best ending available — play it plainly: she is given paper at a desk with a man sitting outside the door, and she works for eleven hours, and she is good at it, and the page that goes down the pass is in her hand. Then the couriers come up, and the party goes down with the fair copy as their contract said, and Coll Rannoch says something about the road, and that is the end.
loot: The fair copy of the Almanac, carried down the pass at thaw, which was always the contract
A page of errata, bound in or not

npcsInvolved.name: Ilsabet Wray, 54
npcsInvolved.description: First up the ladder into the burning loft on the seventh evening. Out through the postern on the seventh night and four hundred yards into the pass before she sits down because she cannot do it. Confesses to C3 and C8 presented together and to nothing else. The confession is a collapse: she does not stand up, does not justify herself well, and does not name pride as the reason even though it was.
npcsInvolved.motivation: See caseFile → culprit. She asked for one season to correct the tables quietly. He said there was no time and that he would bind the errata in and put his own name to the House's negligence. She went up to ask him again. He did not turn round.

npcsInvolved.name: Halva Onn, 40
npcsInvolved.role: Archivist / Holder of the last seal
npcsInvolved.description: The only person left in the building with a seal, and the last decision of the campaign is hers as much as the party's. She will not use it lightly and she does use it, and she writes a line under it recording exactly what she has done and why so that whoever comes after her knows. That line is the most characteristic thing anybody does in this campaign.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Two hundred years of record, kept honestly, including the record of the one time she bent the rule.

npcsInvolved.name: Corwin Tace, 47
npcsInvolved.description: Cleared of the murder, finished by the letters, and consequently the only person in the hall on the last night with nothing left to weigh. He argues for binding the errata in, bluntly, and it is the best thing he does in the campaign and nobody thanks him for it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Having lost everything on day five, he discovers on day eight that he can say what he thinks.

npcsInvolved.name: Oriel Fenn, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Has fed every person in this building three times a day for eight days while they suspected each other. Stops in the doorway with a dish in her hands when the accusation is made and does not put it down until it is over. Cooks breakfast the next morning as usual, for everybody, including the woman in the room with a man outside the door.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Twelve people fed, whatever else is happening.

npcsInvolved.name: Merrit Doane, 22
npcsInvolved.description: Wrong at the top of his voice for six days, silent at the accusation, and the person in the hall who cries when the confession comes — which nobody expects, including him. He is twenty-two, the dead man was the only person who ever took him seriously, and he has just found out that the answer was somebody who checked his arithmetic every week.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have been useful. He was not, and he will be, eventually, and not this winter.

npcsInvolved.name: Sennet Vole, 70
npcsInvolved.description: Opens his eyes when the party stands up, which he has not done in front of anybody in four days, and closes them again when it is over. If C8 was lost, he is the substitute: he can place the study argument between the quarter and the half by the chimes, and he heard somebody on the servants' stair at about a quarter past nine, and he has been waiting six days for someone to ask.

npcsInvolved.name: Nan Gaddy, 38
npcsInvolved.description: Up in the loft when the lamp goes over, brought down by the woman the party is about to accuse. Sits on an upturned tub in the yard with a blanket round her being told off by the cook, and says the only funny thing anybody says in the last two days, and everybody needs it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get her breath back and finish the washing.

npcsInvolved.name: Wat Ormery, 45
npcsInvolved.description: Knows how a roof fire runs and says the one thing that saves the building. Sits outside a door for two nights afterwards with a lamp and a book he does not read, and does not once speak to the person on the other side of it, because he has decided that would be a cruelty either way.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Everyone to thaw alive. He manages it, including her.

rewards.gold: The party's contract fee, paid at thaw as agreed: 150 gp between them, plus their keep for the winter, plus whatever the village of Ambry Vale presses on them for Ewan Barr, which is about 20 gp and a great deal of food.
items: The fair copy of the Almanac, carried down Coldharrow Pass at thaw — which was always the contract
A page of errata, bound in or not, sealed with the Archivist's seal and a line beneath it recording exactly what she did and why
Ardwen's day-books, thirty-one volumes, if the party asks for them, which Halva Onn will grant
The party's own reputation in Ambry Vale, which is worth more in that province than any of the above
rewards.story: Eight days, twelve residents, one death, and one fixed answer that was written down before any of it started. The party either named Ilsabet Wray with the evidence in their hands, or named somebody else and watched the riders take them at thaw, or ran out of days and went down the pass with it recorded as a fall. And separately — because these were always two problems and not one — the eastern hundreds either got a page of errata bound into their Almanac in time to plant on the right date, or they did not, and there is a hundred of poor country somewhere in the east that will find out about it in the spring.

twists: The fire in the loft is an accident and stays an accident. A lamp on a beam, a tired hand reaching for a blanket, and there is no second crime in this campaign.

Ilsabet Wray goes up the ladder first, without hesitating, and pulls Nan Gaddy out from behind the burning lines — twenty-four hours before the party names her. She is not a monster and the accusation has to be made anyway, and both of those are true at once.

She does not run for the pass. She goes four hundred yards and sits down against a rock and cannot make herself go on and cannot make herself go back, and if the party comes out after her she says so.

The confession requires exactly C3 and C8 together and nothing else will do it — not a perfect Persuasion roll, not intimidation, not correctly naming her. A party that has the right answer and not the right evidence gets a quiet 'no' and one more night.
Ardwen's errata sheet named the House and never named her. She killed him for a document that would have protected her, and the party has known this since the third day and she has not.

The best available ending is that the woman who falsified the tables computes the correction, at a desk, with a man sitting outside the door, and the page that goes down the pass to save the eastern harvest is in her handwriting.
dmTips: THE CONFESSION IS C3 PLUS C8 AND NOTHING ELSE. This is the caseFile's contract and the last place the DM will be tempted to break it. A player who names Wray correctly with no evidence gets an ordinary tired woman saying no. A natural 20 on Persuasion gets a no. Being cornered gets a no. If C8 was destroyed in the ash-pan, accept C3 plus Sennet Vole's timing plus a reconstructed timeline — same weight, harder road — but do not accept less than that, and do not invent a new clue to rescue the party.

PLAY THE CONFESSION WITH PITY AND KEEP IT SHORT. She stays sitting. She does not justify herself well. She does not say the word 'pride'. Three or four sentences and then she stops, and nobody in the hall makes her finish. Resist every instinct toward a villain's monologue, a moment of defiance, or a tragic aria — the whole design of this campaign is that the answer is small and sad.

RUN THE FAILURE STATE STRAIGHT IF IT COMES. A wrong accusation that the House accepts is a real ending: the riders take the accused at thaw, Wray tries the postern, and a letter arrives two years later. Do not have an NPC step in with the truth at the last second, do not offer a second accusation, and do not reset. A fair-play mystery that cannot be lost was never fair, and the players will know the difference.

THE FIRE IS AN ACCIDENT. Do not make it arson, do not have anyone set it to destroy evidence, and answer the party's investigation of it honestly on a DC 12: a lamp, a beam, and a hand. If the C4 coat was still up there, it burns, and the case does not need it.

END ON THE ARITHMETIC AND NOT ON THE CONFESSION. The last scene of this campaign is a page of errata and a sealed quire-case going down the pass, because the harvest was always the larger harm and the campaign said so in its own synopsis. Give the errata argument real table time; it is the House deciding to say in print that it was wrong, which is the hardest thing anybody in this building does.

DO NOT LET THE TWO THREADS RESOLVE EACH OTHER. Naming the murderer does not fix the tables and fixing the tables does not name the murderer. Both, either or neither is a legitimate ending and the DM should be entirely willing to close the campaign on a solved murder and a lost crop, or the reverse.

OFFER THE BEST ENDING WITHOUT PUSHING IT. If Wray is alive and in the building, she is the best computer in the province and she will do the correction if asked. Do not have an NPC suggest it. Let a player think of it, and if nobody does, let the correction be done imperfectly by Merrit Doane over eleven hours, which saves about half the crop and is its own kind of ending.

THERE IS NO TRIAL AND NO EXECUTION. She goes to her room, Wat Ormery sits outside it with a lamp and a book he does not read, and at thaw the riders take her down the pass. The campaign ends with the party going down the same road with a quire-case, and Coll Rannoch saying something about the road, and nothing else.

SAY THE COUNT OUT LOUD AT THE END. Eight days. Twelve residents. Nine clues, of which the party found however many they found. Three herrings. One answer, which was written down in data/campaigns/reckoning/campaign.json before the first session and did not change. Players who lost a clue to a clock deserve to be told that the clock was real and that the file has been sitting there the whole time.

PACE IT AS TWO SESSIONS: the fire and the seventh night; then the accusation and the fair copy. Give the accusation as much table time as it wants — this is the scene the whole campaign has been building toward and it is twelve people at a table by lamplight, which is enough.
